subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage:
Rafiq, you'll laugh. My second week in Chennai, my Tamil was about six words, and I needed a mop. At the hardware shop I told the owner, "Hello, I'm Payal, new in the building upstairs," and then I started acting. Hands gripping a stick, pushing it back and forth across the floor. He nodded, very confident, and brought me... a broom. I did it again, bigger, even made a squeezing motion for the bucket. He brought a bucket. Just a bucket.
Then I remembered my phone. I found a photo of a mop, held it up and said, "This one?" He laughed so hard, slapped his forehead, and said the Tamil word slowly for me, twice. Now I point, show a picture, and then check: "This? Yes?" It saves a lot of brooms.

qa.q: What did the shop owner bring the first time Payal mimed?
qa.a: He brought a broom.

qa.q: How do you think Payal felt when the owner brought just a bucket?
qa.a: Payal probably felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed, though the way the story is told suggests it also felt funny looking back. 😅

qa.q: What does Payal do now to avoid mix-ups?
qa.a: Point, show a picture on the phone, and then check with "This? Yes?" before buying.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have seen the miming?
qa.a: He seemed confident he understood each time, so the mime misled him until the photo made it clear, which is why he laughed and taught the word.

grounding: A worker new to a city uses mime and pointing to ask for something, finds gestures can mislead, and checks with a picture and a confirming phrase.

passage:
From his rented flat in Indiranagar, Saurabh held his hands apart in front of the laptop. "The new display stand should be about this wide, okay? Not bigger."
On the other end, Nikita squinted. Her screen showed Saurabh's face, a ceiling fan and the tips of two fingers at the very edges of the frame. The video stuttered, and his hands froze mid-air.
"About... how wide?" she asked. "I can see one thumb."
"This wide!" He spread them again, further this time, forgetting the camera.
Nikita wrote down "large" and frowned. The shop's corner was tiny.
Two days later the carpenter's drawing arrived: a stand nearly two metres across. Saurabh groaned. On the next call he typed "90 cm" in the chat, then held a quick pencil sketch up to the camera.
Nikita laughed. "Now that I can see."

qa.q: What could Nikita see of Saurabh's hands?
qa.a: She could see the tips of two fingers at the very edges of the frame.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she wrote down "large"?
qa.a: Nikita felt unsure and a bit uneasy, since she couldn't really see the gesture and knew the shop's corner was tiny.

qa.q: What fixed the confusion on the next call?
qa.a: Typing the exact size, 90 cm, in the chat and holding up a quick sketch, so the size no longer depended on cropped hands.

qa.q: What would have changed if they had met in the shop?
qa.a: Nikita could have seen the full width of his hands against the real corner, so the size would likely have been clear from the start.

grounding: On a video call, hand descriptions get cropped or frozen and are misread, so typed words and a sketch reduce confusion.

passage:
The paying-guest room had one wobbly desk and a plastic chair too low for it, and Sahil's project report was due on Friday. By Wednesday afternoon he had been hunched over the laptop for six hours, chin nearly on the keyboard.
Santosh, back from his shift, dropped his bag. "You look like you're asleep sitting up. Taking it easy?"
"Easy?" Sahil straightened and winced; his neck cracked. "I haven't stopped since breakfast."
Santosh looked again: the cold tea, the pile of printouts, the red mark on Sahil's forearm from the table edge. "Sorry. From the door it just looked like slouching."
He folded his own pillow and wedged it on the chair to raise the seat, then propped the laptop on two dictionaries. "Twenty minutes, then we walk to the tea stall. Non-negotiable."
Sahil laughed and, for once, sat up straight.

qa.q: What did Santosh use to raise the laptop?
qa.a: He propped the laptop on two dictionaries.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when Santosh asked if he was taking it easy?
qa.a: Sahil felt stung and a little defensive, since he hadn't stopped since breakfast; he was also clearly sore and tired.

qa.q: What small changes did Santosh make, and why do they help?
qa.a: Raising the seat with a pillow, propping up the laptop and planning a walk after twenty minutes, which ease strain on the body and lift the mood.

qa.q: Why did Santosh first read the posture as laziness?
qa.a: From the door he only saw a slouch, not the cold tea, the printouts and the mark on the forearm that showed hours of work.

grounding: Hunching over a laptop for hours can look lazy to others while it is really focus and fatigue; a better seat, a raised screen and breaks help.

passage:
In her first week at the block development office in Tirupattur, Keerthana met two officers. The first, Mr. Selvam, leaned so far back in his chair during her briefing that it creaked, hands behind his head, eyes half closed. She walked out sure he thought her a waste of time.
The second, a woman officer from the district, sat bolt upright, stood very close at the file cabinet and fired quick questions. Keerthana felt she was being tested.
At lunch under the neem tree, Yamini, who had worked there six years, laughed. "Selvam sir leans back when he's relaxed with you. He does that only with people he likes. And Madam stands close with everyone; that's just how she talks."
Keerthana frowned. "So how am I supposed to know?"
"Watch what they do over a month. Who helps you. Who remembers what you said."

qa.q: Where did Keerthana and Yamini eat lunch?
qa.a: They ate lunch under the neem tree.

qa.q: What did Keerthana feel after the briefing with Mr. Selvam?
qa.a: Keerthana felt dismissed and discouraged, reading his leaned-back posture as boredom with her, though it might instead have been relaxed comfort.

qa.q: What does Yamini advise Keerthana to watch?
qa.a: What the officers do over a month: who helps her and who remembers what she said.

qa.q: Why might Yamini read Selvam's posture differently from Keerthana?
qa.a: Yamini has worked there six years and knows he leans back only with people he likes, while Keerthana had just one briefing to judge by.

grounding: Bosses' postures signal status and attitude differently from person to person, so behaviour over time says more than body position.

subtype: Restless pacing at work or in waiting rooms [Regulating]
passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm
Interview day. Writing it down before I forget how it felt.
I got to the office forty minutes early (Ammi's rule), and the waiting area had six chairs and a glass wall. I couldn't sit. I walked from the water cooler to the window and back, maybe thirty times. The receptionist kept glancing up. Another candidate, a guy called Deepak, finally said, "You're making me nervous, yaar," and laughed, but I could see he half meant it.
So I asked the receptionist if I could step out. I walked once round the building in the sun, breathed slowly, told my hands to unclench. Came back and sat, feet flat.
They called Hafsa at 11:20. My voice didn't shake. Don't know yet if I got it. But I didn't pace into the room, which feels like a win.

qa.q: How many chairs did the waiting area have?
qa.a: The waiting area had six chairs and a glass wall.

qa.q: Why couldn't Hafsa sit down in the waiting area?
qa.a: Hafsa felt nervous and restless before the interview, and pacing was a way to burn off that energy.

qa.q: What helped Hafsa more than pacing in the waiting area?
qa.a: Stepping out, walking once round the building, breathing slowly and then sitting with feet flat. 🙂

qa.q: How did the pacing affect Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak, another candidate waiting, found it unsettling; he joked, but it made him more nervous too.

grounding: Pacing before an interview burns nervous energy but can look like impatience to others; stepping out for a walk and breathing helps more.

subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
passage:
The lunch rush at the small restaurant in Porto was at its worst when Rafael, the sous-chef, shouted across the kitchen that Paulo had ruined a whole tray of sea bass. Paulo felt the heat climb up his neck. The words ready on his tongue were not ones he could take back.
He untied his apron and walked out the back door without a word.
Rafael stared after him. "Unbelievable. He just leaves?" The dishwasher shrugged.
In the alley, Paulo pressed his back to the cold wall and counted his breaths until his jaw loosened. Five minutes. Then he went back in.
"Rafael. I walked out because I was about to say something stupid. I'm sorry I didn't say that first. The fish was overdone; I'll redo the tray."
Rafael held his gaze for a moment, then nodded at the stove. "Next time, just say 'two minutes.' Go."
Paulo tied his apron back on.

qa.q: What did Rafael say Paulo had ruined?
qa.a: A whole tray of sea bass.

qa.q: Why did Paulo walk out of the kitchen?
qa.a: Paulo felt angry and stung by the shouting and was afraid of saying something he couldn't take back, so he left to cool down.

qa.q: What made Paulo's walkout end well?
qa.a: He came back after five minutes, explained why he had left, apologised for not saying so first and offered to redo the tray.

qa.q: How did Rafael see the walkout at first?
qa.a: Rafael read it as disrespect, saying "Unbelievable. He just leaves?", until Paulo returned and explained.

grounding: Leaving a heated exchange can prevent regrettable words, but it reads as disrespect unless the person returns with a calm explanation.

passage:
The platform at Dadar was packed at nine, and the man who had followed Noor down the stairs was now shouting at her, swaying, far too close.
Ayesha stepped in front of her friend almost without thinking, shoulders squared. Her first urge was to shout back. The man's face twisted, and he took a step nearer.
Something in Ayesha's head said: not this. She kept her body between them but turned sideways, not squaring up to him, and caught Noor's wrist. "We're going," she said, low and steady, and pulled her along the platform towards the lit booth where two railway police officers stood.
"That man in the grey shirt is harassing her," Ayesha told them, pointing back. One officer walked towards the stairs at once.
Noor's hand was shaking in hers. Ayesha didn't let go until they were inside the ladies' compartment and the doors were closing.

qa.q: Where were the two railway police officers standing?
qa.a: They stood at the lit booth along the platform.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she stepped in front of Noor?
qa.a: Ayesha felt protective and angry, with an urge to shout back, and also afraid as the man stepped closer.

qa.q: Which choice kept both friends safer, and why?
qa.a: Turning sideways, leading Noor away and reporting the man to the railway police, because it avoided a fight and put people with authority in charge.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to be led away?
qa.a: Noor was shaken, her hand trembling, but being held and taken to help likely made her feel safer and less alone.

grounding: Stepping between a friend and a threat is caring, but moving away and calling the authorities is the wiser protection than escalating.

passage:
After my father's long illness and the project that swallowed that whole winter, I stopped being someone people could reach. I'm Gargi, the loud one from college, and suddenly I ate lunch at my desk, answered in single words, jumped when a door slammed. Some colleagues decided I'd become arrogant after the promotion.
Vandana didn't decide anything. She kept leaving a second cup of tea on my desk at four, no questions. Once she said, "You don't have to talk. I just want you to know I'm around." Another day she slipped me the number for the counselling service our office offers and said, "Only if and when you want."
It took me three weeks to call. I still don't fully know what that winter was: grief, tiredness, something else. But I remember who didn't push.

qa.q: What did Vandana leave on Gargi's desk at four?
qa.a: A second cup of tea, with no questions.

qa.q: What might Gargi's startling and single-word answers have shown?
qa.a: Most likely Gargi was worn out and grieving after the father's illness and a hard project; it could also have been exhaustion alone, which is why Gargi still isn't sure.

qa.q: What made Vandana's support helpful?
qa.a: She stayed present through small, steady gestures, didn't push Gargi to talk, and offered the counselling number for whenever Gargi was ready.

qa.q: How did some colleagues read Gargi's withdrawal?
qa.a: They decided Gargi had become arrogant after the promotion, misreading the pulling back as pride.

grounding: Pulling back and startling easily after a hard period may reflect grief or exhaustion, and supportive people offer patience and professional help instead of pushing.

passage:
First Friday. At the team lunch the conversation dried up while everyone waited for the dosas. Dolma pulled out her phone and scrolled, thumb flicking. Ramesh, halfway through a story about his daughter's school play, trailed off and looked at his plate.
The next Wednesday. Ramesh stopped by her desk. "Can I ask something? At lunch you seemed bored with us. Was my story that bad?"
Dolma's face went hot. "No! Honestly, I grab my phone whenever there's a silence. It's like holding something. And one message was the vendor about Monday's shipment."
"Ah. From across the table it just looked like you'd left."
Third Friday. The silence came again. Dolma's phone buzzed. She glanced at it, then said, "Sorry, the vendor again, one minute." She replied, turned the phone face down and asked, "Ramesh, how did the play end?"

qa.q: What was Ramesh's story about?
qa.a: His daughter's school play.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's face go hot when Ramesh asked his question?
qa.a: Dolma felt embarrassed and a little guilty, seeing that the scrolling had looked like boredom when it was a comfort habit in silences, plus one real work message.

qa.q: What did Dolma change on the third Friday?
qa.a: She gave a short explanation before replying, turned the phone face down afterwards and went back to Ramesh's story.

qa.q: How did the scrolling look to Ramesh at the first lunch?
qa.a: Ramesh felt hurt and ignored, as if Dolma had left the table, and he trailed off mid-story.

grounding: Picking up a phone in awkward moments can be comfort or urgent work but is often read as disrespect, and a short explanation prevents hurt.

subtype: Rubbing temples and neck at work [Expressing]
passage:
So here's a small thing that stuck with me. Last month we had a four-hour planning meeting, no windows, and I didn't notice I kept rubbing my temples, then the back of my neck, round and round. My manager, Ramesh, stopped mid-slide and said, "Yusuf, you've been rubbing your head for twenty minutes. Headache, bored, or do you hate this plan?" Everyone laughed, including me.
Truth is, it was a bit of all three. The lights were giving me a headache, the budget part was dull, and I did think the timeline was mad. He couldn't have known which from my hands. So he asked, and then he called a ten-minute break for everyone.
I got water, told him about the timeline outside, and we fixed it before lunch. Now when I see someone rubbing their neck in a meeting, I just ask.

qa.q: How long was the planning meeting?
qa.a: It was a four-hour planning meeting, with no windows.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling while rubbing the temples and neck?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a mix: headachy from the lights, bored by the budget part and worried that the timeline was mad.

qa.q: What did Ramesh try, and why did it help?
qa.a: He asked kindly what the rubbing meant instead of guessing and called a ten-minute break, which let Yusuf rest and raise the timeline problem.

qa.q: How might the others in the room have read the rubbing?
qa.a: They might have guessed tiredness, pain or disagreement, since the gesture alone couldn't tell them which one it was.

grounding: Rubbing the neck or temples in a long meeting may signal tiredness, tension or headache, so asking kindly and offering a break beats guessing.
